newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief to raise warnings on big telecom mergers.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief to raise warnings on big telecom mergers.

text.p: In what is being billed as a major speech on merger policy, the top U.S. phone regulator is expected to raise warning flags Thursday about the kind of deal being proposed between AT&T Corp. and SBC Communications Inc.

Outgoing Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt already has been raising questions about such a merger, which, if completed, would create a giant company with a stock market value of $110 billion.

It would be the largest corporate merger in U.S. history, although neither company has commented on whether they are holding merger talks following the big 1996 law designed to open the communications business to new competition.

Attorney Nicholas Allard of Latham & Watkins, Hundt's old law firm, expects the FCC chief to deliver this message to the telecommunications industry: "Don't misinterpret the telecom act. Don't do whatever you want to do. You don't have a blank check.
"We're going to insist on more competition rather than more monopoly," Allard said.

The FCC has billed the speech as a "major" address. Agency officials declined to comment on the content. Hundt last week said a mega-merger of AT&T and regional Baby Bell SBC remains "unthinkable" in most antitrust experts' views.

In a clear reference to AT&T and SBC, Hundt urged regulators "to take an extremely cautious and wary approach" toward proposed mergers involving markets in which previous laws barred the entry of "potentially formidable competitors."

Up until last year's communciations law, SBC and other regional Baby Bells were barred from the U.S. long-distance business, while carriers like AT&T effectively were shut out of the local phone market.
But the new law set forth a mechanism for doing away with legal barriers that have kept the Bells out of the long-distance business since the break-up of the old Ma Bell phone monopoly in 1984.
The new law also was intended to break open local phone monpolies controlled by the Bells.

AT&T, the No. 1 long-distance company, serves more than 80 million residential customers and 10 million businesses. SBC dominates local phone service in a seven-state area stretching from Texas to California.

"The government knows competition is going to come to the big cities first. And since SBC controls some of the largest metropolitan areas, AT&T in its rumoured merger with SBC wouldn't be competing in most of those markets," said analyst Scott Cleland of Legg Mason Precursor Group, the research arm of the Baltimore-based brokerage firm.
Among the big cities already on SBC's turf: Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, Houston, Dallas and San Diego.
